analytic.title: MemGuard-RW: Improved Real-Time Memory Bandwidth Regulation within a Hypervisor

div.p: Memory bandwidth is a critical factor in the performance of DRAM-based computing architectures, particularly in memory-intensive computations. Modern multi-core processors share critical resources, such as main memory and cache, which impact the predictability of real-time systems due to resource contention. Techniques like memory access regulation, cache partitioning, and static hypervisors aim to mitigate this contention.

This paper presents an improvement of a memory control mechanism based on MemGuard, named MemGuard-RW, designed and implemented within a hypervisor. MemGuard-RW uses two performance counters for measuring the memory accesses, one for memory readings and another one for writings, thus decreasing the pessimism on the original memory access budget from MemGuard. Additionally, we extend the MemGuard schedulability analysis considering the two-counter approach. To evaluate the effectiveness of the implementation and analysis, we deployed FreeRTOS as a guest alongside three stress-generating guests, measuring the interference experienced by the FreeRTOS instance and comparing the analysis with two counters with the original analysis with one counter, using modern benchmarks. The results demonstrate that the proposed mechanism successfully regulates memory accesses, showing its potential for enhancing the predictability and performance of real-time systems in multi-core environments. Our proposed analysis with two counters reduces the upper bound of around 20% for tasks having medium and high memory usage.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: T HE low timing predictability of multi-core processors is a significant problem in real-time systems due to contention for shared memory resources [1]. It concerns safetycritical applications such as the ones found in automotive and aviation industries, where bounded execution time is crucial [2].

The complexity of modern safety-critical systems, often requiring heterogeneous multi-core processors, has led to the need for robust shared resource management and isolation at the system software level [1], [3]- [5]. These systems integrate both safety-critical and general-purpose functions (mixed criticality), making predictable performance essential. Hypervisors like Bao [6] and Jailhouse [7], known for their lightweight, static partitioning and strong isolation capabilities, can be suitable for these environments. Such lightweight hypervisors can isolate the guest real-time operating systems (RTOS), preventing them from directly accessing physical resources with negligible run-time overhead (without the need for emulation of paravirtualization) [6], [7]. Thus, it is possible to create different mixed criticality domains that are isolated.

Several recent works have extended the existing lightweight hypervisors with spatial and temporal isolation techniques, such as cache partitioning [5], and memory bandwidth regulation [8]- [10]. Memory bandwidth regulation is one of the most efficient techniques to prevent two or more cores from overloading the shared memory bus and interfering with the execution of safety-critical tasks. Traditional memory regulation approaches, such as the well-known MemGuard [11], usually use performance monitoring counters (PMCs) to track memory accesses and stop the cores that exceed the assigned bandwidth reservation (i.e., budget). The budget usually treats reads and writes from/to memory equally. However, writes into the main memory take more cycles than reads [12]. This creates pessimism in the budget assignment and, consequently, in the schedulability analysis.

This paper addresses this gap by improving the original MemGuard approach. It extends MemGuard to regulate both memory reads and writes at the hypervisor level and introduces a new schedulability analysis. Our work differs from [8], which implements the original MemGuard with a single counter in the Bao hypervisor but does not propose any new analysis. It also differs from [12], which uses two separate counters for memory regulation to prevent Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks but does not introduce any new analysis.
In this paper, we make the following contributions:

• We design and implement an extended version of Mem-Guard (named MemGuard-RW) with two counters within the Bao hypervisor, and evaluate the implementation in a modern multi-core platform (Raspberry Pi 4, featuring an ARM A72 processor with 4 cores). • We provide a new schedulability analysis considering a memory bandwidth budget from two different performance counters, one for reads and another for writings. • We evaluate and compare the new schedulability analysis with the one from [13] using memory profiles from modern benchmarks. Our proposed analysis with two counters reduces the upper bound of around 20% for tasks having medium and high memory usage. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II discusses the background of memory regulation and virtualization. Section III reviews some related works. Section IV introduces the task and system models. Section V presents the schedulability analysis, and Section VII evaluates its effectiveness and characterizes empirically the memory usage of different benchmarks. Section VI discusses the design and implementation of MemGuard-RW in Bao using the ARM A72 processor. Finally, Section VIII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: This section first discusses the software-and hardwarebased approaches for ensuring the predictable execution on multi-core platforms with shared hardware resources and then introduces two main system-level software components used in our work: MemGuard bandwidth regulator and Bao hypervisor.

A. Software-and hardware approaches for predictability Software methods are those implemented at the operating system or hypervisor level. They focus on managing resources such as memory, cache, and CPU bandwidth through software techniques like cache coloring [1], [14], [15], software bandwidth regulation (e.g., MemGuard [11]), and memorycentric scheduling [4], [16]- [18]. Hardware techniques, on the other hand, involve physical changes or control at the architectural level of the processor or memory controller. Techniques such as cache locking, memory bank allocation, and hardware-based regulation bandwidth (e.g., Intel's MBA) are some examples. Hardware approaches can provide more precise and low-level control of resources (e.g., cache locking), they can handle physical constraints like energy as described in [19], and also offer stronger guarantees on predictability and real-time performance due to their direct interaction with the hardware. Unfortunately, these hardware features are often unavailable on many of today's commercial off-theshelf processors. However, there is an increasing integration of quality of service features in the SoC to enable low latency for highly latency-sensitive cores and allow hardware bandwidth regulation.

div.head: B. MemGuard
div.p: MemGuard is one of the most well-known software solutions for memory bandwidth regulators used in real-time systems [11]. It ensures that critical tasks receive a guaranteed amount of memory bandwidth. Each core receives a portion of the bandwidth, isolating and preventing excessive memory requests from other cores. When a particular core depletes its assigned budget and if there is no way to reclaim some more budget from the reclaiming component, that core is suspended until the next period, when a new budget is assigned. Implemented originally at the operating system (OS) level, Mem-Guard uses the PMCs of each core for event counting (e.g., last-level cache writebacks). MemGuard provides a minimum service rate for each core, while the best-effort applications take advantage of remaining and unused bandwidth.

The schedulability analysis with one counter presented in [13] proposes a method to compute the task's worst-case response time for multiprocessors running under MemGuard. The analysis was later improved by Mancuso et al. by using the precise budget information available at system design time [20] (the analysis in [13] pessimistically assumes that the budgets of the interfering cores are evenly distributed).

div.head: C. Bao hypervisor
div.p: Bao is an open-source lightweight hypervisor that statically partitions hardware resources [6]. It assigns dedicated memory, CPU, and I/O devices to each guest (or Virtual Machine -VM) by the time it starts. Thus, there is no need for a global scheduler, reducing the system complexity and decreasing the run-time overhead. Bao has a two-stage translation for static memory assignment, direct pass-through I/O handling, and a basic inter-VM communication mechanism via shared memory and asynchronous notifications. It also supports cache coloring to partition the last-level caches (LLCs), therefore preventing shared cache interference. The Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC -for ARM-based platforms) is used for forwarding interrupts to the hypervisor, which re-injects them into the appropriate VM. Bao has been used in many recent works, and due to its flexibility, open-source, and active community, we have chosen it for our implementation and experimental tests.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: Many techniques have been proposed to mitigate the problems related to shared memory resources in real-time systems running on multi-core processors [1], [4].

Kritikakou et al. adopts a progress-aware approach to control the inter-core memory interference on multi-core platforms [21]. This approach makes use of a run-time control mechanism to monitor the execution of the high-criticality tasks and applies a safety condition to check whether the slack time is sufficient to continue the execution of the highcriticality tasks. If not, the low-criticality tasks running on the other cores are suspended, and the high-criticality tasks continue to execute in isolation with no inter-core interference. This approach has been extended in [22] to dynamically adapt to the current online temporal properties of the system and, based on these properties, activate or skip the next observation points, thereby reducing the regulator's runtime overhead.

A recent work by Gomes et al. used MemGuard to create a bandwidth regulation within Bao hypervisor [8]. It laid down the main functionalities that make the regulation possible, such as the Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU) configuration and the communication among the VMs. However, it only uses one counter to monitor memory accesses for each created VM. In this work, we use two counters (one for readings and one for writings) with two budgets and propose a new schedulability analysis.

Farshchi et al. proposed a hardware module designed to regulate bandwidth at the core level, reducing interference between cores [2]. It provides a way to control the bandwidth of individual and multiple cores, improving bandwidth utilization and timing predictability for real-time tasks, and allowing besteffort tasks to better utilize the memory system bandwidth. Zuepke et al. proposed MemPol, a regulation mechanism that operates externally to the cores, monitoring performance counters for application in main memory at a finer microsecond scale via debug interfaces [10]. Ye et al. proposed a system designed to manage and mitigate shared cache and memory bus contention in multicore processors, using performance counters to regulate the memory bandwidth [23]. Crespo et al. uses the same idea, but their regulation addresses critical and non-critical workloads [9]. Intel also proposed the Memory Bandwidth Allocation Architecture (MBA) in complement to the Cache Allocation Technology (CAT) to provide a programmable per-core memory bandwidth regulation.

Mirosanlou et al. strike a balance between average performance and predictable worst-case execution time (WCET) in memory access for real-time embedded systems by proposing a novel memory controller that can take advantage of pipelining between different commands [24]. Sohal et al. introduce profile-driven approaches allowing empirical estimation of the shared resource usage in real-time applications in bandwidthregulated commercial-off-the-shelf systems [25]. Dagieu et al. modified the existing MemGuard kernel module to work in virtualized environments [26]. The original MemGuard [11] was designed for the x86 architecture and has been ported to the ARMv8 architecture. The solution includes modifications to the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) in Linux to synchronize with MemGuard, allowing bandwidth regulation at the core and guest levels in a virtualized environment.

Overall, all the related works discussed above do not differentiate readings and writings for memory regulation mechanisms. In this paper, we explore this feature and propose both the implementation and analysis.

div.head: IV. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We introduce the system and task model used in this paper.

div.head: A. System model
div.p: We assume a multicore system with m cores that share a single bus and main memory. We assume that the memory accesses generated by each core are arbitrated based on the first-come, first-served policy: after processing the current memory transaction, the controller moves to the memory transaction requested by the next core. The scheduled memory transactions are atomic and cannot be preempted. We assume that there are two types of memory transactions: read and write. Each read memory access takes at most L R cycles (time units), called worst-case read latency, and each write memory access takes at most L W cycles (time units), called worst-case write latency. We assume that L W ≥ L R , and define η = L W /L R as the ratio of possible writes in one read.

In the considered multicore system, we regulate the memory bandwidth (i.e., the amount of memory that can be read or written to and from memory per time unit) on a percore basis. Accesses to the main memory are monitored using two separate counters: the read counter and the write counter. In our implementation, these counters are derived from PMU events, specifically tracking memory load and store operations. Read accesses are measured using memory load events, while write accesses are tracked using memory store events. Since writes can be buffered before being served to the main memory, and obtaining precise per-core write statistics at the memory controller level can be challenging. Instead, we approximate write contributions using store instruction counts and use cache coloring to isolate memory regions across cores, improving attribution accuracy.

We consider that all cores have the same regulation period P which starts and ends on each core synchronously. The i-th core is assigned a budget Q i ≥ 0, which is the maximum allowed memory access time (i.e., number of memory cycles) within a period P . For simplicity, we will drop the index in Q i for the core under analysis when there is no confusion. Each access to the main memory is subtracted from the core's memory budget. The budget of each core is fully restored at the end of each period. If a core tries to access the memory when it does not have enough budget, it will be stalled until the start of the next period. We consider that the memory is not overloaded, that is,

The regulation period and budgets are expressed in processor cycles. Figure 1 presents schematically how two-counter memory regulation works. Inconsistencies can appear when a read (or a write) operation starts at P -L R +1 (resp. P -L W +1), causing the write to overflow in the next period or to have a negative remaining budget. We forbid these operations at the end of the regulation period and include this overhead in its duration P .

div.head: B. Task model
div.p: We consider a partition-based scheduling with m aperiodic tasks and cores, where each task is pre-assigned to a particular core and all jobs generated by a task may only execute upon this particular core (i.e., no migration). Our analysis assumes a single task per core but it can be extended to multi-tasks system as in [13]. Task τ has a worst-case execution time when running alone C (i.e., no other tasks on the same core and no co-runners on the other cores). We assume that computation and memory accesses are non-overlapping (i.e., in-order execution). We denote by N R and N W the number of reads and writes of task τ , and by N = N W + N R the total number of memory accesses. We define τ 's worst-case execution time as C = C e + C m where C e is the computation time and C m is the memory access time. The latter can be expressed as
div.formula: C m = C R + C W , where C R = N R • L R
div.p: is the read memory access time, and C W = N W • L W is the write memory access time. Task τ worst-case response R is the longest time from the release of the task to its completion.

Determining the exact memory pattern of a task can be complex in practice as it may require the full knowledge of the tasks' execution traces, which depend on both task inputs and hardware state. We assume that neither the positions nor the orders of memory accesses are known a priori: our analysis computes an upper bound of the task's worst-case response time. Furthermore, write requests are buffered and served in blocks from the LLC, causing write operations issued in the main memory to be delayed if there is a cache hit. We assume the cache has a write-through policy to avoid delaying inter-core interference for an unpredictable time. This does not prevent buffering write operations but ensures that operations are in-order. As already observed in [13], the program path with the largest number of memory accesses does not necessarily correspond to the worst-case execution time. It is therefore necessary to establish separately an upper bound for task execution time and its number of memory accesses. Moreover, the number of read and write operations might also vary. For the sake of our analysis, it is necessary to upper bound the number of writes N W and the total number of all memory accesses N , and consider N R = N -N W .

In what follows, we extend this analysis by differentiating between read and write latencies to obtain tighter upper bounds.

The analysis considers two types of memory stall: (i) due to the memory budget overrun (called memory bandwidth regulation stall), and (ii) due to concurrent memory access from the other cores (called inter-core contention stall). In one regulation period, a core can issue up to Q memory accesses, meaning that the worst-case stall cannot be greater than P -Q.
The memory bandwidth regulation stall occurs when the core under analysis issues Q memory cycles and then is suspended until the end of the current regulation period, for the remaining P -Q cycles.

The inter-core contention stall occurs when the core under analysis is delayed by the interfering memory accesses from the other cores. In the worst situation, it must wait until the writes from all other m -1 cores are processed. This is because the main memory controller implements the firstcome, first-served policy and because it takes longer to process a single write than a single read operation, L W > L R . div.head: VI. DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: In this section, we detail the implementation of a twocounter-based memory regulator at the hypervisor level.

The proposed memory bandwidth regulation method is based on MemGuard [11]. Differently from what we can find in [8], which also used the MemGuard within Bao, in this research, we introduce the division of the Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU) counters, where for each guest RTOS has attributed two counters, one for readings and another one for writing operations. By separating these counters, we can have more control over the given budget for each RTOS.

Every time any RTOS needs to make use of any hardware resource, it relies on the hypervisor to provide the requested service. To allow the counters to perform the described operations, several modifications are required in both the hypervisor and the RTOS. On the RTOS side, each guest is responsible for determining which counters and events it would use, defining the budgets for each operation, combining them into only one final budget, and sending commands to start or stop the counters. These operations are performed using hypercalls from the RTOS to the hypervisor.

When the hypervisor receives a hypercall to configure the counters, its first action is to clear the requested counter to ensure that no values would interfere with the new configuration. The hypervisor then sets the event and budget parameters as specified by the RTOS. Similarly, for requests to start or stop a specific counter, the hypervisor updates the corresponding registers in the PMU for that particular counter.
We added PMU support for the ARM A72 processor (used in our experiments) in Bao and modified it to handle hypercalls to configure, start, and stop PMU counters.

Once a counter overflows, either by reaching the assigned bandwidth of reads or writes, the PMU generates an overflow interrupt. The hypervisor then handles this interrupt (also added by our implementation). The handler checks whether an overflow interrupt happened or not. If so, the handler injects a software-generated interrupt (SGI) into the guest RTOS, which can then resume the suspended task or allow the resuming of the task. The configured events in the counters 0 and 1 of each core were MEM_ACCESS_LD and MEM_ACCESS_ST, which count the number of memory reads and writes. On the guest side, we use FreeRTOS [27] and configure it to handle the SGI interrupt and to issue hypercalls.

Figure 5 shows a general overview of how the described system is structured. The counters within the CPU's PMU are set with the pre-defined budgets for the two counters. This configuration is done from the hypervisor (i.e., Bao). The ARM Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC) handles an overflow interrupt, which passes the control to the interrupt handler. An SGI is then followed to the destination RTOS (i.e., guest).

div.head: VII. EVALUATION
div.p: This section evaluates the runtime performance and analyzes the regulation with two counters. First, we present an experimental evaluation by executing benchmarks on top of our MemGuard-RW implementation running on the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B platform, featuring an ARM A72 processor (Section VII-A). We also compare our proposed approach with two counters with the analysis of one counter using some instances of the CortexSuite benchmarks [28] (Section VII-B).

div.head: A. Experimental evaluation
div.p: Memory access regulation was done by creating specific configurations called profiles. Each profile includes two main settings: a limit (threshold or budget) for read and write operations and a factor that sets the ratio between read and write operations. For example, profile n can have one read operation for every 10.000 write operations, then the budget for this profile was set to 5.010.000 (10.000 reads plus 5.000.000 writes).

In total, 17 distinct profiles composed of budgets ranging from 1.000 to 1.000.000 and factors to read and write operations, varying from 1 to 10 for both reads and writes, were tested to check how the system performed under different conditions on the Raspberry Pi 4 platform using our implementation. The profiles did not have any correlation between them, and the execution was arbitrary. The tests focused on two types of tasks. Non-critical tasks, represented by a bandwidth benchmark [29], which continuously accessed memory to stress the memory bus, and critical tasks, represented by the MSER benchmark from the CortexSuite, which needed predictable timing and were also ported to FreeRTOS. Three instances of the BW benchmark were executed on three different cores, while MSER was assigned to another core, where all tasks were configured with the same priority. To verify how the critical task could perform under the regulation applied to non-critical tasks, the critical task was not regulated, only the non-critical tasks were regulated.
The results compared the performance of three cases:

• Without regulation (C1): No budget was applied to memory accesses. • Regulation type 1 (C2): A new budget was given at the start of each new period. This case simulates a scenario where no replenishment budget is available. • Regulation type 2 (C3): A new budget was provided immediately when a core depletes its current budget. This case simulates a scenario where an application could have an instant reclaimed budget. For non-critical tasks, the time of all benchmarks was measured while running the bandwidth benchmark under two configurations: using one counter keeping track of the event DATA_MEMORY_ACCESS and two counters keeping track of the event MEM_ACCESS_LD and MEM_ACCESS_ST, where the time is given in milliseconds, these values were obtained by using a function in the FreeRTOS to capture the system tick count at both the start and end of the task, then this value is converted into the desired time.

Figures 6(a) and 6(b) illustrate the time taken by the noncritical tasks to complete 200 iterations or jobs, without any delay between them. On the x-axis, we vary the profile configuration. The y-axis represents the time in ms, and also the standard deviation is represented by the black error bars. Figure 6(b) shows the time to complete 200 iterations using two different counters. We can note that the average time to complete has decreased by about 40% in the C2 case, mainly because the regulation mechanism with Memguard-RW is more active (it happens less frequently) than in the case with one counter (which allows the task to run for longer periods). It is important to note that the values in Figures 6(a) and 6(b) represent the total time a non-critical task took to complete all its jobs, not the actual execution time of the task. In other words, they indicate how long the task took to finish, including any interruptions or delays, rather than how much CPU time it consumed. Figure 6(a) shows the case using one counter, where the non-critical task took more time to complete its job because it was interrupted more frequently. In contrast, Figure 6(b) demonstrates that the non-critical task completed its job in less time using two counters, as it experienced fewer interruptions compared to the one-counter approach.

Figure 7 shows the obtained WCET of the critical task, represented by the MSER benchmark, after 10 consecutive executions without any delay between them, using one and two counters. The execution time baseline is 70 ms, which corresponds to the MSER task running alone on the system without interference. The profiles (P) in this figure were arbitrarily selected from the 17 available profiles to demonstrate that, even under regulation in the C2 and C3 cases, where P1-C1 means profile 1 counter 1. The critical task maintained its WCET when using two counters, comparable to the onecounter case (including profiles not shown in the figure). In some cases, such as profiles 3 and 9 (i.e., P3 and P9), the WCET was slightly reduced with two counters.

The regulation has more influence on non-critical tasks because they are less prioritized and more sensitive to changes in resource allocation. The primary goal of MemGuard-RW is to reduce execution time by enforcing memory access regulation, ensuring that non-critical tasks do not interfere with the performance of critical tasks. Similar to the original Mem-Guard, this approach isolates execution environments between tasks, allowing predictable and efficient task execution. With two counters, the system improves the execution time of noncritical tasks without negatively impacting the critical tasks' Fig. 7: WCET of a critical benchmark (MSER) by the regulation done on the non-critical tasks. On the x-axis, we represent the case with one and two counters (e.g., P1-C1 and P1-C2). performance, which maintains or even reduces its WCET. This demonstrates an optimized and balanced resource management strategy and better system utilization.

Our model assumes a simplified environment where each core runs a single task, which simplifies things to focus on the basic idea of memory access regulation. In practice, the presence of multiple tasks per core introduces additional complexity, such as task-level interference and context switching, which can impact the accuracy of the memory access counts.

We acknowledge that this assumption of a single task per core might not fully reflect the behavior of systems with multiple concurrent tasks. In such environments, the behavior of PMU counters could become more challenging to interpret, as different tasks could generate varying access patterns that influence memory bandwidth.

B. Schedulability analysis evaluation 1) Benchmark profiling: Both analyses require the total execution time and the number of accesses to the DRAM of each program. We profile the LLC miss count for both reads and writes using Cachegrind, a tool from Valgrind [30].

We use the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B's ARM A72 processor characteristics in our experiments. We consider that each core has a frequency of 2.3 GHz, stalls on each memory request, and has an L1 data cache of 2 16 kB sets with a cache block size of 64 bytes and an L1 instruction cache of 3 16 kB sets with a cache block size of 64 bytes. The processor has a shared LLC of size 1 MB with a cache block size of 64 bytes. We assume that there is no interference within the LLC. The main memory has a read frequency 1/L R = 28 MHz and a write frequency 1/L W = 14 MHz, which makes η = 2. For the one counter analysis, we consider that the latency L is the write latency L W . Access to the main memory occurs when the data is not in the cache.
2) Results with CortexSuite: In this subsection, we compare the worst-case response time upper bounds calculated using the analyses with one [13] and two counters (Section V).

We compute the analytic worst-case response time on instances of the CortexSuite Benchmark covering different memory intensities and read-write repartition: kmeans libl, me, pca, spc, sphinx, and srr. Each instance has three sizes depending on its memory usage: small, medium, and large.

Using the task profiling described in the previous subsection, we extract the LLC total miss count N , and the LLC read and write miss counts N W and N W , and the execution time C. Figure 8 presents the miss rate and the proportion of read miss for all benchmarks. We consider that a task has a small impact on memory when its miss rate is below 0.5%, a medium impact on memory between 0.5% and 1%, and a high impact over 1%.

To compute the access times of each instance, we used the profiled access counts. For the analysis with one counter, the time taken by memory accesses is C m = N • L W . For the analysis with two counters, the read memory time is merged with the write memory time:
div.formula: C m = N R • L R + N W • L W . The computation time for both analyses is given by C e = C -C m .
div.p: For experiments, we run the instances of the CortexSuite benchmark presented earlier one by one with m = 4. The regulation period P is set to 1 ms. The srr small instance has been omitted due to its insignificant number of cache misses.

Figure 9 presents the results of the benchmark after both analyses. The y-axis shows the normalized response times in relation to the lowest calculated result (with full budget Q=P ). The x-axis shows the budget of the analyzed core, expressed as a percentage of P . We make the following observations. First, both analyses follow the same pattern: an exponential decrease followed by a flat area to a final decrease. The new analysis merges with the old one during the final decrease. The meeting point is at high budgets, around 80%. The flat area represents the transition from the regulation case to the contention case, and the final decrease corresponds to the moment when the memory time finishes earlier than the computation time. When the task quickly runs out of computation, the plateau is reduced to a minimum.

Second, during regulation (the first decrease), the analysis with two counters will always provide better results than the analysis with one counter. This is because a read access counts for L R in the new analysis, dividing by η each read access from the old one. Note that for instances with low read proportion, the regulation part of both curves is almost identical due to this phenomenon.

Finally, during contention (the flat area), the analysis with one counter provides better results when the proportion of read accesses is less than 50%. This is because each write access is stalled for (m -1) • L W • η, increasing the number of periods with the worst-case stall. When the task transitions from regulation to contention case for the new analysis, the execution time rises to reach the flat area. This is due to the pessimism of the analysis on write accesses, which uses less computation and adds more periods of worst-case stalls.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper proposed MemGuard-RW, an extension of the original MemGuard memory bandwidth regulation mechanism to use two PMCs, one for reading and another for writing. We have implemented MemGuard-RW in the Bao hypervisor and evaluated it using a modern multi-core platform (Raspberry Pi 4 with an ARM A72 processor with four cores). Important components were implemented, such as the PMU configuration, as well as interrupts, hypercalls within Bao, and SGI handling in the FreeRTOS (our guest). We also proposed a new schedulability analysis considering two counters.
Analytic results present better upper bounds when using two counters when there is a high number of LLC misses, around 20% in the flat region.

Experimental results, as illustrated in Figures 6(a) and 6(b), demonstrate that the number of counters used in the regulation mechanism significantly affects task performance. For noncritical tasks, the regulation increased the time required to complete their jobs, nearly doubling it in the one-counter case and increasing it by up to 40% depending on the regulation strategy applied. This behavior is attributed to more frequent interruptions caused by the regulation mechanism. In contrast, when two counters were employed, non-critical tasks experienced fewer interruptions, resulting in a shorter overall completion time. For critical tasks, the use of two counters preserved the worst-case completion time observed with the one-counter configuration, and in some cases, even reduced it. These results highlight the flexibility and effectiveness of the proposed memory bandwidth regulation approach in managing task execution without compromising real-time guarantees. As future work, we plan to investigate the impact of having multiple tasks monitored by the PMCs, as well as their interaction with the Memguard-RW mechanism. While Memguard-RW is designed to improve memory bandwidth regulation by differentiating between read and write accesses, handling write buffering, and enabling dynamic budget allocation, we have yet to evaluate its effectiveness in more complex scenarios involving multiple tasks.
